doc.title: Leslie Johnson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Childhood response to jazz and family not musical
summary: Johnson recalls the energy of New Orleans jam sessions and dancing as a six-year-old to Kid Ory and Ellington; her parents were not into jazz and she heard it on local radio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: That’s what I think the appeal is that it has a quality that just draws you in and it energizes you. I think that’s the thing that I really love about traditional jazz and early music. And when I would go down to New Orleans and be at Preservation Hall for instance, we would stay up all night of course at jam sessions. But the music was so energizing that you didn’t get tired. You’d go all night and then the next night go all night. But the music just had such vitality. And that, I can remember first hearing it when I was a little kid and it had that quality for me as a six and seven year old child. I distinctly remember hearing certain tunes by Kid Ory and certain tunes by Duke Ellington, and dancing. And that was my response.
Were your parents — were they into it or not?

No. Not at all. Not at all. My mother loved music but it was more classical, and she wasn’t all that tuned into it, although she became quite a jazz fan as I got involved in it and went to New Orleans and really did the whole bit, and was reasonably knowledgeable about it and my family sort of came into it. But no it wasn’t a family that was oriented around music.
Where did you hear it then?

I just heard it on the radio. It was played on — there was a local DJ who liked early jazz, although at that time it wasn’t as early as it is now. There were still players around like Red Allen, I mean we’re talking about the forties and fifties. So it was still on the radio.
